Two of the four participants, one LTR and one RTL, both with a colonial history, were in the analysis sample.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. info.title: Postcolonial English Exposure and the Visual Mental Timeline

author.affiliation:
Institute of Psychology
								Beaconhouse National University

text.text: The spatial-temporal association of response codes (STEARC) effect describes faster responses when past-related stimuli map onto the left and future-related stimuli map onto the right.

This exploratory study asked whether an English-official-language or colonial-history background is associated with a smaller STEARC effect, and whether any such association is specific to the visual modality.
Trial-level data came from 96 participants.
An attention check retained 70 participants and 135 participant-by-modality scores.
STEARC was the mean response time (RT) of incongruent trials minus that of congruent trials, computed with a fixed left-to-right mapping for every participant.
A mixed model showed a colonial history by modality interaction, F(1, 130) = 8.64, p = .004, p FDR = .012.
The visual contrast was 515 ms, 95% CI [ 854, 176].
After adjustment for reading direction the contrast was 391 ms, 95% CI [ 846, --64], p = .091, and the Bayes factor was inconclusive (BF01 = 1.78).
Colonial history and reading direction overlapped strongly (φ = .59), and 17 of the 26 participants with a colonial history read right to left.
Resampling checks supported the unadjusted contrast but not clearly the adjusted contrast, and the interaction did not reach significance without the attention filter.
The results are consistent with, but do not establish, an influence of postcolonial English exposure on the visual mental timeline.
We treat them as a hypothesis for a design in which colonial history and reading direction are crossed, and we give sample sizes for that design.
People use space to think about time.
In many cultures the past is placed on one side of a horizontal axis and the future on the other.

This mapping is called the mental timeline. Torralbo et al. (2006) showed that people project time onto space in a flexible way. Santiago et al. (2007) then found that people respond faster with the left hand to past-related words and with the right hand to future-related words than under the reverse mapping. Ouellet et al. (2010) examined whether temporal words orient spatial attention or prime a congruent left or right response. Ulrich and Maienborn (2010) found the same congruency pattern when participants processed past-related and future-related sentences.
text.formatted: This mapping is called the mental timeline. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Torralbo et al. (2006)</ref> showed that people project time onto space in a flexible way. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Santiago et al. (2007)</ref> then found that people respond faster with the left hand to past-related words and with the right hand to future-related words than under the reverse mapping. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Ouellet et al. (2010)</ref> examined whether temporal words orient spatial attention or prime a congruent left or right response. <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Ulrich and Maienborn (2010)</ref> found the same congruency pattern when participants processed past-related and future-related sentences.

text.text: The pattern is often called the spatial-temporal association of response codes (STEARC) effect.
It is a standard behavioral index of the mental timeline.

The direction of the mental timeline is not fixed. Tversky et al. (1991) found that speakers of languages with different writing directions laid out temporal sequences in different directions. Fuhrman and Boroditsky (2010) found that English speakers arranged time from left to right and Hebrew speakers from right to left in a nonlinguistic task. Bergen and Chan Lau (2012) compared English, Mainland Chinese, and Taiwanese Mandarin speakers and linked the spatial layout of time to native writing direction. Casasanto and Bottini (2014) had Dutch speakers complete a space-time task with instructions and stimuli in mirror-reversed text and found a reversed pattern of response times. Pitt and Casasanto (2020) proposed that concepts of time follow the correlations that people experience between space and time, so that reading experience shapes the timeline.

(1991)</ref> found that speakers of languages with different writing directions laid out temporal sequences in different directions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Fuhrman and Boroditsky (2010)</ref> found that English speakers arranged time from left to right and Hebrew speakers from right to left in a nonlinguistic task. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bergen and Chan Lau (2012)</ref> compared English, Mainland Chinese, and Taiwanese Mandarin speakers and linked the spatial layout of time to native writing direction. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Casasanto and Bottini (2014)</ref> had Dutch speakers complete a space-time task with instructions and stimuli in mirror-reversed text and found a reversed pattern of response times. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Pitt and Casasanto (2020)</ref> proposed that concepts of time follow the correlations that people experience between space and time, so that reading experience shapes the timeline.

text.text: The spatial-numerical association of response codes (SNARC) effect, first reported by Dehaene et al. (1993), shows a related dependence on reading habits. Zebian (2005) found a weaker reversed pattern in Arabic-English biliterates than in Arabic monoliterates. Shaki et al. (2009) found no reliable association in Israeli participants, who read words right to left and numbers left to right.

(2009)</ref> found no reliable association in Israeli participants, who read words right to left and numbers left to right.

text.text: Cultural variation of this kind raises a sampling issue. Henrich et al. (2010) showed that behavioral science draws heavily on a narrow set of populations. Núñez and Sweetser (2006) documented an Aymara construal of time in which the future lies behind the speaker, and Boroditsky et al. (2011) reported differences between English and Mandarin speakers. Núñez and Cooperrider (2013) review how spatial construals of time vary across cultures.

(2011)</ref> reported differences between English and Mandarin speakers. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Núñez and Cooperrider (2013)</ref> review how spatial construals of time vary across cultures.

text.text: Many STEARC studies compare groups that each have one dominant reading direction.

Readers who use more than one direction are common in much of the world, and they offer a natural test of the idea that reading experience shapes the timeline. Schneider (2003) describes how English took root in postcolonial settings and developed into local varieties.
text.formatted: Readers who use more than one direction are common in much of the world, and they offer a natural test of the idea that reading experience shapes the timeline. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Schneider (2003)</ref> describes how English took root in postcolonial settings and developed into local varieties.

text.text: In many of these countries English remains an official language.
A person from such a country may read a right-to-left script such as Urdu in one setting and left-to-right English in another.
We call this combination postcolonial English exposure.

If reading experience shapes the mental timeline, as Pitt and Casasanto (2020) propose, a reader with opposing experiences could show a less polarized timeline than a reader with one dominant direction.
text.formatted: If reading experience shapes the mental timeline, as <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Pitt and Casasanto (2020)</ref> propose, a reader with opposing experiences could show a less polarized timeline than a reader with one dominant direction.

text.text: The SPOT-L2 dataset does not measure exposure directly.
It records whether English is an official language in each participant's country of origin, and this marker serves here as a coarse proxy.
Modality offers a second angle.
Visual stimuli are written, so reading direction is engaged directly.
Auditory stimuli carry no script.
If reading experience drives a difference between groups, the difference should be larger in the visual modality than in the auditory modality.
We therefore ask whether any association with colonial history is specific to the visual modality.
STEARC is a difference score, and RT distributions are right skewed.
Group comparisons can therefore depend on a few extreme participants (Ratcliff, 1993).
text.formatted: Group comparisons can therefore depend on a few extreme participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Ratcliff, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: We address this with explicit bounds, a pre-agreed trim, medians, rank-based tests, and resampling, and we report the share of participants whose score is positive.
Because the study is exploratory, we state expectations as directions and not as confirmatory predictions.
Under an exposure account, participants with a colonial history should show a smaller STEARC score than participants without one, and the difference should be larger in the visual modality.
Under a reading-direction account, the same pattern should appear but should vanish once reading direction is controlled.
The two accounts make the same prediction for the unadjusted contrast.
They differ for LTR readers with a colonial history, who should resemble other LTR readers under the reading-direction account but not under the exposure account.
A further problem is overlap.
In the present sample most participants with an Englishofficial background read right to left.
A difference between groups could reflect reading direction, English exposure, or both.
We therefore present the study as exploratory and hypothesis generating.
We ask three questions.
First, is an English-official or colonial-history background associated with a different STEARC score overall?
Second, is any difference specific to the visual modality?
Third, does a visual difference remain after reading direction is controlled?
We show the overlap between the two factors before any test, we quantify how much evidence the data hold against the confound, and we specify the design that would resolve it.
This study is exploratory and hypothesis generating.
The analysis followed a pre-agreed plan that fixed the dataset, the outcome, the predictor, the covariate, the exclusion rules, and a family of three focal tests.
The replication file (Story3_Replication.Rmd) reproduces every number, table, and figure in this article from the trial-level data file.
Several steps went beyond the plan.

They are a standardized difference, model-based estimates and diagnostics, rank-based and resampling checks, a planning calculation for a follow-up study, and one sensitivity scenario added after a data audit.
Each is labelled where it appears, in line with the distinction between confirmatory and exploratory analyses (Wagenmakers et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Each is labelled where it appears, in line with the distinction between confirmatory and exploratory analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Wagenmakers et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The data file held 7,680 trials from 96 participants.
Each participant contributed 80 trials, We kept participants with an average quiz accuracy of 60 or above on the 0 to 100 scale.
This attention check retained 70 of the 96 participants (73%) and excluded 26 (27%).
The retained participants had a mean age of 24.76 years (SD = 6.53, range 18-46).
They included 38 women, 29 men, and 3 nonbinary participants.
Of the 70 participants, 49 read left to right (LTR) and 21 read right to left (RTL).
English-official or colonial-history status was coded 1 for 26 participants and 0 for 44 participants.
The 17 RTL participants with a colonial history reported Urdu (14), Punjabi (2), or Saraiki (1) as their language.
The 9 LTR participants with a colonial history comprised six first-language English speakers with London as origin and one speaker each of Gujarati, Igbo, and Sinhalese.
The comparison group was mostly LTR (n = 40) and included 30 German-language participants.
The 4 RTL participants without a colonial history reported Hebrew (2), Arabic (1), or Persian (1).
The predictor was the variable that marks English as an official language in the participant's country of origin.
The variable that codes colonial past was identical to it in this sample, so only one was entered.
We label it English-official or colonial history throughout.
The covariate was reading direction (LTR or RTL).
It is the main confound and the only covariate that is necessary.
Language distance and all other covariates were excluded.
Language distance had almost no real variance in this sample.
The other covariates were null after FDR correction in an earlier exploratory screen and would only add noise.
STEARC was computed for each participant and modality as the mean RT of incongruent trials minus the mean RT of congruent trials.
Congruent trials were Past-Left or Future-Right responses.
We applied this LTR-style mapping to every participant.
Positive values therefore mean slower responses against the expected mapping.
For RTL readers, values near zero or below zero can be read as a smaller or reversed effect.
We did not use the STEARC column in the data file because it holds one untrimmed value per participant collapsed across modality, and it cannot test a modality moderation.
We kept RTs from 200 to 10,000 ms, which removes anticipatory presses and stalled trials. Ratcliff (1993) discusses the case for cutoffs of this kind in RT analysis.
text.formatted: We kept RTs from 200 to 10,000 ms, which removes anticipatory presses and stalled trials. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Ratcliff (1993)</ref> discusses the case for cutoffs of this kind in RT analysis.

text.text: We then applied a perparticipant trim at ±3 SD on log RT.
The trim was kept only if it removed 15 percentage points of trials or fewer beyond the absolute bounds.
A participant-by-modality score was dropped when either congruency cell was empty.
We used R 4.3.3 (R Core Team, 2024) with the tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019), lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), and lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
text.formatted: We used R 4.3.3 (R Core Team, 2024) with the tidyverse <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Wickham et al., 2019)</ref>, lme4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref>, and lmerTest <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Kuznetsova et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The primary model was a linear mixed model.
STEARC was the outcome.
English-official or colonial history, modality, and their interaction were fixed effects.
Reading direction entered as an additive covariate, and participant had a random intercept.
Type III tests used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.
We tested the visual contrast in ordinary least squares models, unadjusted and adjusted for reading direction.
A Wilcoxon rank-sum test served as a rank-based check.
The focal family held three tests, namely the main effect of colonial history, the colonial history by modality interaction, and the adjusted visual contrast.
We corrected their p values with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).
text.formatted: We corrected their p values with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: The significance level was .05, two-sided.
A non-significant adjusted p value cannot show whether the adjusted contrast is absent or simply unmeasured.
We therefore computed a BIC-based Bayes factor (Wagenmakers, 2007), which rests on the approximation described by Raftery (1995).
text.formatted: We therefore computed a BIC-based Bayes factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Wagenmakers, 2007)</ref>, which rests on the approximation described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Raftery (1995)</ref>.

text.text: Model 1 added colonial history to a visual model that already held reading direction, and Model 0 omitted it.
BF01 equals exp((BIC 1 -BIC 0 )/2).
Values between 1/3 and 3 were treated as inconclusive.
Sensitivity analyses repeated the key tests with no attention filter, with absolute RT bounds only, with extreme visual scores removed (|z| above 3), and with LTR readers only.
For the visual contrast we also report a standardized difference based on the pooled SD (Lakens, 2013).
text.formatted: For the visual contrast we also report a standardized difference based on the pooled SD <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Lakens, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary analyses used the primary model to estimate cell means and the interaction contrast with Satterthwaite intervals, and we inspected residuals with a normal Q-Q plot and a residual plot.
We estimated the visual contrast with a Hodges-Lehmann shift and a Wilcoxon interval (Hodges & Lehmann, 1963).
text.formatted: We estimated the visual contrast with a Hodges-Lehmann shift and a Wilcoxon interval <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Hodges & Lehmann, 1963)</ref>.

text.text: We ran permutation tests with 10,000 permutations.
The unadjusted test shuffled colonial-history labels across all participants, and the adjusted test shuffled them within reading-direction groups.
Permutation p values equal (1 + count) / (10,000 + 1), which avoids values of zero (Phipson & Smyth, 2010).
text.formatted: Permutation p values equal (1 + count) / (10,000 + 1), which avoids values of zero <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Phipson & Smyth, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: We also computed percentile bootstrap intervals from 5,000 resamples of participants (Efron, 1979).
text.formatted: We also computed percentile bootstrap intervals from 5,000 resamples of participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Efron, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: Random seeds were fixed.
After the plan was fixed, we checked the file for duplicated records.
Two pairs of participants had identical RT sequences across all 80 trials.
Independent respondents cannot produce identical sequences.
Two of the four participants, one LTR and one RTL, both with a colonial history, were in the analysis sample.
The primary analysis kept these records, as agreed.
A post hoc sensitivity scenario removed all four participants.
We computed the participants per cell that a crossed follow-up would need, using the residual SD of the adjusted visual model, 80% power, and a two-sided alpha of .05 in a two-sample t test.
We used the observed raw (515 ms) and adjusted (391 ms) differences and half of each, because exploratory subgroup contrasts tend to be overestimated (Gelman & Carlin, 2014).

Their 5,600 trials were screened with the absolute RT bounds, which removed 139 trials (2.5%).
The per-participant trim at 3 SD on log RT removed 14 further trials (0.26 percentage points).

The result therefore depends on the attention filter.

This exploratory study asked whether an English-official or colonial-history background is associated with the STEARC effect, and whether any association is specific to the visual modality.
The colonial history by modality interaction was reliable and survived FDR correction.
In the visual modality, participants with a colonial history showed a smaller STEARC effect than participants without one.
The median was 122 ms in the first group and 428 ms in the second.
The auditory modality showed no comparable difference.
Participants from English-officiallanguage or colonial-history backgrounds showed a smaller visual STEARC effect, although this difference could not be shown to be independent of reading direction.
These findings are consistent with, but do not establish, an influence of postcolonial English exposure on the visual mental timeline.
Two accounts fit the visual pattern.
The first is a reading-direction account.
The task applied a fixed left-to-right mapping to every participant.
RTL readers would score near zero or below zero under that mapping if their timeline runs in the opposite direction (Fuhrman & Boroditsky, 2010).
text.formatted: RTL readers would score near zero or below zero under that mapping if their timeline runs in the opposite direction <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Fuhrman & Boroditsky, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The RTL group with a colonial history fits this account, with a mean of 9 ms.
The second is an exposure account.
Readers who use both a right-to-left script and left-to-right English have experience with opposing directions.

Under the correlations in experience view (Pitt & Casasanto, 2020), such experience could produce a less polarized timeline. Shaki et al. (2009) reported a comparable pattern for numbers in readers with mixed habits.
text.formatted: Under the correlations in experience view <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Pitt & Casasanto, 2020)</ref>, such experience could produce a less polarized timeline. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Shaki et al. (2009)</ref> reported a comparable pattern for numbers in readers with mixed habits.

text.text: The data cannot choose between the accounts.
Because most participants with a colonial background were RTL readers, the two factors could not be statistically separated in this sample.
The phi coefficient was .59, and two visual cells held fewer than eight scores.
After adjustment for reading direction, the visual contrast was 24% smaller in magnitude and its interval included zero.
The Bayes factor of 1.78 was inconclusive.

The rank-based and resampling checks agreed with the parametric result for the unadjusted contrast, but not clearly for the adjusted contrast, where the bootstrap interval excluded zero and the permutation test did not.
The LTR-only contrast stayed close to the unadjusted estimate, at 507.5 ms, and a pure reading-direction account would not predict that.
The estimate rests on seven participants, however, and it was not reliable (p = .083).
We regard it as a pointer for future work and not as evidence for either account.
The visual pattern agrees with the idea that written stimuli engage reading experience more directly than spoken stimuli do.
The auditory contrast was small, with means of 8 ms and 30 ms.
Two cautions apply.
The primary model entered reading direction as an additive term, so it did not allow reading direction to act differently in each modality.
A modality-specific reading-direction term was not part of the plan.
The interaction therefore tests colonial history by modality after an additive adjustment, and it does not rule out a reading-direction by modality pattern.
In addition, five visual scores were missing because of empty congruency cells.
The results bear on three broader points.
First, STEARC studies that use groups with one dominant reading direction cannot show how mixed-direction experience is combined.
Samples that include readers of several scripts, as in SPOT-L2, offer a way to ask this question.
They can do so only if reading direction and cultural background are measured separately.
Second, a country-level marker such as English as an official language is easy to code but hides differences in individual exposure.
Studies of postcolonial populations should record which languages and scripts participants read, the ages at which they began, and how often they read each one.
These measures follow from the correlations in experience principle (Pitt & Casasanto, 2020), because they describe the experience that the principle says should shape the timeline.
text.formatted: These measures follow from the correlations in experience principle <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Pitt & Casasanto, 2020)</ref>, because they describe the experience that the principle says should shape the timeline.

text.text: Third, exploratory findings need to be reported with their dependence on analytic choices.
The attention filter, the trim, and the treatment of duplicated records each moved the estimates, and Table 6 and Figure 7 show the full set.
text.formatted: The attention filter, the trim, and the treatment of duplicated records each moved the estimates, and Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">6</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_9">7</ref> show the full set.

text.text: The interaction stayed reliable under every choice except the removal of the attention filter, and the adjusted visual contrast was not reliable under any choice.
The cells were small.
The visual modality held seven LTR scores with a colonial history and three RTL scores without one.
The result also depended on the attention filter.
Without it the interaction fell to p = .056 and the adjusted contrast to 177.3 ms.
The filter was pre-agreed and removed 27% of participants, so this dependence matters for interpretation.
The predictor was coarse.
English-official background in the country of origin does not measure individual exposure, proficiency, age of acquisition, or reading practice.
Reading direction was also a binary proxy.
Statistical control for a coarse proxy of a latent construct can leave residual confounding (Westfall & Yarkoni, 2016), so even a fully adjusted contrast would not isolate exposure.
text.formatted: Statistical control for a coarse proxy of a latent construct can leave residual confounding <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Westfall & Yarkoni, 2016)</ref>, so even a fully adjusted contrast would not isolate exposure.

text.text: The groups were also not homogeneous.
Six of the 26 participants with a colonial history were first-language English speakers with London as origin, and the comparison group held 30 German-language participants among 44.
The comparison therefore mixes differences in language, country, and script with colonial history, and it samples a narrow part of the world (Henrich et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The comparison therefore mixes differences in language, country, and script with colonial history, and it samples a narrow part of the world <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Henrich et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The outcome was skewed.
Visual STEARC scores had long right tails, so we reported medians and a rank-based test beside the means.
The mixed model was singular.
Robust mixedmodel checks and residual diagnostics are planned as a separate step and are not part of this workflow.
The data audit found two pairs of participants with identical RT sequences.
The conclusions held when these participants were removed, but the source of the duplication should be traced before the data are shared.
Finally, all claims are associational.
Colonial history and reading direction are not separable here, and the data cannot support a causal statement about exposure.
The only way to separate colonial history from reading direction is a sample in which the two diverge.
We propose a crossed design.
It would compare LTR readers with colonial-English backgrounds, for example from India, Nigeria, or Singapore, with LTR readers without such backgrounds.
It would add an RTL comparison.
The three focal tests, the exclusion rules, and the wording of claims should be locked before data collection.
The planning calculation used a residual SD of 662 ms.
With 80% power and a two-sided alpha of .05, a two-sample contrast needs 27 participants per cell if the true difference is 515 ms and 46 per cell if it is 391 ms.
If the true differences are half as large, the needs rise to 105 and 181 per cell.
Estimates from exploratory subgroup contrasts tend to be inflated (Gelman & Carlin, 2014), so the larger figures are the safer basis for a sample size justification (Lakens, 2022).
text.formatted: Estimates from exploratory subgroup contrasts tend to be inflated <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gelman & Carlin, 2014)</ref>, so the larger figures are the safer basis for a sample size justification <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Lakens, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A follow-up should also measure exposure directly, with proficiency, age of acquisition, and reading habits for each script.
Figure 8 shows how power rises with sample size for each contrast.

Participants from English-official-language or colonial-history backgrounds showed a smaller visual STEARC score, and the difference could not be separated statistically from reading direction.
We treat this result as a hypothesis for a design in which colonial history and reading direction are crossed.
Until such data exist, the pattern should be read as consistent with an exposure account and not as proof of one.
